meta.title: Nasrins Weg
meta.source: Lesson titles, grammar and story beats aligned with vhs-Lernportal A1/A2 Deutschkurs (DVV) and the 'Nasrins Welt' video blog; scenes extrapolated where needed.

lessons.storyArc: Nasrin Fani, newly arrived from Afghanistan, walks into her first Integrationskurs at the Volkshochschule in Hamburg. She is nervous, introduces herself to the teacher Frau Lehmann and to her classmates Rafael (Brazil), Magdalena (Poland), Melek (Turkey) and Yonas (Eritrea), and learns that people in northern Germany say 'Moin'.
lessons.setting: Volkshochschule Hamburg, classroom
grammarFocus: Personalpronomen ich, du, Sie, er, sie
Verb in second position in statements

items.context: Nasrin stands in front of the class on her first morning. Frau Lehmann asks her to introduce herself.
items.promptEn: Good morning! My name is Nasrin Fani.
items.answerDe: Guten Morgen! Ich heiße Nasrin Fani.
items.rule: 'heißen' means 'to be called' and is the standard way to give your name. With 'ich' the verb ends in -e. 'Guten Morgen' is used until about 10–11 a.m., after that people switch to 'Guten Tag'.
alternativeAnswers: Guten Morgen! Mein Name ist Nasrin Fani.

items.context: Frau Lehmann asks Nasrin where she is from.
items.promptEn: I come from Afghanistan.
items.answerDe: Ich komme aus Afghanistan.
items.rule: 'aus' (from) is used for origin. Most country names have no article, so nothing changes after 'aus'. 'kommen' with 'ich' takes the ending -e. Compare 'der Iran' or 'die Türkei', which DO take an article: 'aus dem Iran', 'aus der Türkei'.

items.context: Frau Lehmann greets Nasrin at the door: 'Guten Morgen, Frau Fani! Wie geht es Ihnen?'
items.promptEn: Thanks, fine. And you? (formal)
items.answerDe: Danke, gut. Und Ihnen?
items.rule: 'Wie geht es Ihnen?' uses the formal Dative pronoun 'Ihnen' (to you). You answer with the same case: 'Und Ihnen?'. With friends it would be 'Wie geht's dir?' – 'Und dir?'.
alternativeAnswers: Danke, mir geht es gut. Und Ihnen?
Danke, es geht mir gut. Und Ihnen?

items.context: In the break Nasrin sits next to Rafael. They are both students, so they use 'du'.
items.promptEn: Where are you from? (informal)
items.answerDe: Woher kommst du?
items.rule: 'Woher' asks about origin (wo = where, her = from here toward the speaker). In a W-question the question word is first and the verb second. 'du' takes the ending -st.

items.context: Nasrin introduces Rafael to Melek.
items.promptEn: He comes from Brazil and speaks Portuguese.
items.answerDe: Er kommt aus Brasilien und spricht Portugiesisch.
items.rule: 'sprechen' is a vowel-changing verb: e becomes i in the du- and er/sie-forms (du sprichst, er spricht). 'kommen' is regular: er kommt. Languages are capitalised nouns in German.

items.context: Yonas asks Nasrin how good her German is. She wants to be modest.
items.promptEn: I speak a little German.
items.answerDe: Ich spreche ein bisschen Deutsch.
items.rule: 'ein bisschen' means 'a little/a bit' and never changes its form. Languages take no article: 'Deutsch', not 'das Deutsch'. In the ich-form 'sprechen' keeps its e: 'ich spreche'.
alternativeAnswers: Ich spreche etwas Deutsch.
Ich spreche nur ein bisschen Deutsch.

items.context: Yonas walks up to Nasrin and asks: 'Bist du Nasrin?'
items.promptEn: Yes, I am Nasrin. And who are you? (informal)
items.answerDe: Ja, ich bin Nasrin. Und wer bist du?
items.rule: 'sein' is irregular: ich bin, du bist, er/sie ist, Sie sind. 'Wer' asks for a person (who). Because Yonas used 'du', Nasrin answers informally too.

items.context: The school secretary comes in and Nasrin needs to ask her name politely.
items.promptEn: What is your name? (formal)
items.answerDe: Wie heißen Sie?
items.rule: Germans ask 'HOW are you called', so it is 'Wie', not 'Was'. The formal 'Sie' always takes the infinitive form of the verb (heißen) and is always Capitalised.
alternativeAnswers: Wie ist Ihr Name?

items.context: Nasrin has just been introduced to Magdalena and wants to say something friendly.
items.promptEn: Nice to meet you.
items.answerDe: Freut mich.
items.rule: Short for 'Es freut mich, Sie/dich kennenzulernen' (it pleases me to meet you). Germans usually drop the 'es' and just say 'Freut mich'. It works for both 'du' and 'Sie'.
alternativeAnswers: Freut mich, dich kennenzulernen.
Freut mich, Sie kennenzulernen.
Sehr erfreut.

items.context: Class is over. Nasrin says goodbye to Rafael and Melek at the bus stop.
items.promptEn: Bye, see you tomorrow!
items.answerDe: Tschüss, bis morgen!
items.rule: 'Tschüss' is the everyday informal goodbye; 'Auf Wiedersehen' is formal. 'bis' + a time word means 'see you ...' (bis morgen, bis später, bis bald). No verb is needed.
alternativeAnswers: Tschüs, bis morgen!
Auf Wiedersehen, bis morgen!

lessons.storyArc: Nasrin registers her four-year-old son Arian at the Kita. The director Frau Schneider hands her a form: Nasrin spells her surname, gives her address and phone number and talks about her family – her husband Jamal, her nine-year-old daughter Mina and her parents, who still live in Afghanistan.
lessons.setting: Kita 'Sonnenblume', director's office

items.context: Jamal has come along to the Kita. Nasrin introduces him to Frau Schneider.
items.promptEn: This is my husband Jamal.
items.answerDe: Das ist mein Mann Jamal.
items.rule: 'Mann' means both 'man' and 'husband' – 'mein Mann' always means 'my husband'. Possessive 'mein' has no ending before masculine and neuter nouns in the Nominative; it takes -e before feminine and plural nouns (meine Frau, meine Kinder).

items.context: Frau Schneider asks where the family lives.
items.promptEn: We live in Hamburg.
items.answerDe: Wir wohnen in Hamburg.
items.rule: With 'wir' the verb is identical to the infinitive: wohnen. 'wohnen' means to live at a place/address; 'leben' is used for living in a broader sense (a country, a lifestyle). Cities take 'in' with no article.

items.context: Frau Schneider looks up from the form: 'Haben Sie Kinder?'
items.promptEn: Yes, I have a daughter and a son.
items.answerDe: Ja, ich habe eine Tochter und einen Sohn.
items.rule: 'haben' takes a direct object in the Accusative. Feminine 'eine Tochter' looks the same as in the Nominative, but masculine 'ein Sohn' becomes 'einen Sohn' – only masculine articles change in the Accusative.
alternativeAnswers: Ja, ich habe zwei Kinder, eine Tochter und einen Sohn.

items.context: Frau Schneider asks about Mina, who is not being registered but is listed as a sibling.
items.promptEn: My daughter is nine years old.
items.answerDe: Meine Tochter ist neun Jahre alt.
items.rule: German expresses age with 'sein' + number + 'Jahre alt' (to BE nine years old), not with 'haben'. 'Tochter' is feminine, so the possessive is 'meine'. In casual speech you can drop 'Jahre alt': 'Meine Tochter ist neun.'
alternativeAnswers: Meine Tochter ist neun.

items.context: Nasrin practises the form's questions with Jamal at home, playing the official.
items.promptEn: Are you married? (formal)
items.answerDe: Sind Sie verheiratet?
items.rule: A Yes/No question starts with the verb in position 1 (Sind Sie ...?), unlike W-questions where the question word comes first. 'verheiratet' is an adjective after 'sein' and takes no ending.

items.context: In class the next day, Nasrin asks Melek about her home.
items.promptEn: Where do you live? (informal)
items.answerDe: Wo wohnst du?
items.rule: 'Wo' asks about a location (where at). Don't confuse it with 'woher' (where from) or 'wohin' (where to). The du-form adds -st to the stem: wohn + st.

items.context: Frau Schneider: 'Wie ist Ihre Adresse?'
items.promptEn: My address is Bergstraße 12, 20144 Hamburg.
items.answerDe: Meine Adresse ist Bergstraße 12, 20144 Hamburg.
items.rule: German addresses go street + house number, then postcode + city. 'Adresse' is feminine, so it is 'meine Adresse'. When you say it aloud, the postcode is read digit by digit: zwei-null-eins-vier-vier.
alternativeAnswers: Ich wohne in der Bergstraße 12, 20144 Hamburg.
Bergstraße 12, 20144 Hamburg.

items.context: Frau Schneider asks about emergency contacts. Nasrin explains where her parents are.
items.promptEn: My parents live in Afghanistan.
items.answerDe: Meine Eltern leben in Afghanistan.
items.rule: 'Eltern' is always plural, so the possessive takes -e: 'meine Eltern', and the verb is the plural form 'leben'. 'leben' (not 'wohnen') is preferred when talking about which country someone lives in.
alternativeAnswers: Meine Eltern wohnen in Afghanistan.

items.context: Arian makes friends with another boy at the Kita. Nasrin asks the boy his age.
items.promptEn: How old are you? (informal)
items.answerDe: Wie alt bist du?
items.rule: 'Wie alt' literally means 'how old'. The verb is 'sein' (bist), never 'haben', because Germans ARE an age rather than HAVE it.

items.context: Nasrin shows Frau Schneider a photo on her phone.
items.promptEn: That is my son Arian. He is four.
items.answerDe: Das ist mein Sohn Arian. Er ist vier.
items.rule: 'Das ist ...' is used to point out any person or thing, regardless of gender. Once the noun is known, you refer back with the matching pronoun: 'der Sohn' becomes 'er'. Age without 'Jahre alt' is normal in speech.
alternativeAnswers: Das ist mein Sohn Arian. Er ist vier Jahre alt.

lessons.storyArc: Nasrin learns how to survive in the classroom: asking what a word means, asking the teacher to repeat, and saying she doesn't understand. Frau Lehmann shows a trick for learning articles, so Nasrin covers the flat in sticky notes – 'der Stuhl', 'die Wand', 'das Fenster' – and even labels Mina 'die Tochter'. The course runs Monday to Friday.
lessons.setting: Classroom and the Fani family's flat
grammarFocus: Full present-tense conjugation, vowel change in sprechen
Days of the week and time adverbs (heute, morgen, gestern)

items.context: Frau Lehmann uses a word Nasrin has never heard. Nasrin raises her hand.
items.promptEn: Excuse me, what does 'Wand' mean?
items.answerDe: Entschuldigung, was bedeutet „Wand“?
items.rule: 'bedeuten' (to mean) is the verb for asking about meaning; 'heißen' works too ('Was heißt Wand?'). 'Entschuldigung' is the all-purpose polite opener for interrupting or asking a stranger.
alternativeAnswers: Entschuldigung, was heißt „Wand“?
Entschuldigung, was bedeutet Wand?
Entschuldigung, was heißt Wand?

items.context: Mina tests Nasrin on the sticky notes and points at the table.
items.promptEn: That is not a chair, that is a table.
items.answerDe: Das ist kein Stuhl, das ist ein Tisch.
items.rule: To negate a noun that has an indefinite article (ein Stuhl) or no article, German uses 'kein', not 'nicht ein'. 'kein' takes the same endings as 'ein': kein Stuhl (m), keine Wand (f), kein Fenster (n).

items.context: Frau Lehmann explains the homework quickly and asks: 'Verstehen Sie das?'
items.promptEn: No, I don't understand that. Please speak slowly.
items.answerDe: Nein, ich verstehe das nicht. Bitte sprechen Sie langsam.
items.rule: 'nicht' negates the whole sentence and goes after the object ('das'), at the end. A polite request to 'Sie' is formed with verb + Sie: 'Sprechen Sie ...'. 'kein' would be wrong here because there is no indefinite noun to negate.
alternativeAnswers: Nein, das verstehe ich nicht. Bitte sprechen Sie langsam.
Nein, ich verstehe das nicht. Sprechen Sie bitte langsam.

items.context: Nasrin wants to label the window but doesn't know the German word yet.
items.promptEn: What is 'window' in German?
items.answerDe: Wie heißt „window“ auf Deutsch?
items.rule: German asks 'How is X called in German?' – 'auf Deutsch' means 'in German'. This chunk and 'Was bedeutet ...?' are your two survival questions for learning any new word.
alternativeAnswers: Was heißt „window“ auf Deutsch?
Wie heißt window auf Deutsch?
Was heißt window auf Deutsch?

items.context: Nasrin compares her new course book with Rafael's old pen.
items.promptEn: The book is new, but the pen is old.
items.answerDe: Das Buch ist neu, aber der Kuli ist alt.
items.rule: Adjectives after 'sein' (predicative) never take an ending: neu, alt. 'aber' is a coordinating conjunction in 'position zero' – it does not change the word order, so the verb stays in second place after it.
alternativeAnswers: Das Buch ist neu, aber der Stift ist alt.

items.context: Nasrin asks Rafael and Magdalena together about their habits at home.
items.promptEn: Do you (both) speak German at home?
items.answerDe: Sprecht ihr zu Hause Deutsch?
items.rule: 'ihr' is the plural 'you' for people you address with 'du'. Its ending is -t (sprecht) and, unlike du/er, it does NOT take the vowel change. 'zu Hause' = at home (location).
alternativeAnswers: Sprecht ihr Deutsch zu Hause?

items.context: Jamal asks Nasrin about her timetable so he can plan the Kita pick-ups.
items.promptEn: The course is from Monday to Friday.
items.answerDe: Der Kurs ist von Montag bis Freitag.
items.rule: 'von ... bis ...' (from ... to ...) frames a time span. Days of the week are masculine nouns and are capitalised. No article is needed after von/bis with weekday names.
alternativeAnswers: Der Kurs geht von Montag bis Freitag.

items.context: Frau Lehmann is about to move on, but Nasrin wants to ask something.
items.promptEn: I have a question.
items.answerDe: Ich habe eine Frage.
items.rule: 'Frage' is feminine, so the Accusative article after 'haben' is 'eine' (feminine does not change in the Accusative). This is the polite way to get the floor in class or at an office.

items.context: Mina, doing her own homework, asks: 'Mama, ist Deutsch schwer?'
items.promptEn: German is not easy, but it is interesting.
items.answerDe: Deutsch ist nicht leicht, aber es ist interessant.
items.rule: Adjectives are negated with 'nicht' (never 'kein'), placed directly before the adjective. 'Deutsch' as a language is neuter, so the pronoun that refers back to it is 'es'.
alternativeAnswers: Deutsch ist nicht einfach, aber es ist interessant.
Deutsch ist nicht leicht, aber interessant.

items.context: Friday afternoon. Nasrin leaves the classroom and says goodbye to Frau Lehmann.
items.promptEn: Have a nice weekend! See you Monday.
items.answerDe: Schönes Wochenende! Bis Montag.
items.rule: Wishes like 'Schönes Wochenende', 'Schönen Tag' are short for 'Ich wünsche Ihnen ein schönes Wochenende', so the adjective carries the Accusative ending (-es for neuter 'Wochenende', -en for masculine 'Tag'). 'Bis Montag' = see you on Monday.
alternativeAnswers: Ein schönes Wochenende! Bis Montag.
Schönes Wochenende! Bis Montag!

lessons.storyArc: Nasrin does the weekly shopping at the market and the supermarket, asking for prices in German for the first time. For her video blog 'Nasrins Welt' she tests typical German food – Sauerkraut (sour!), Apfelmus (sweet) and Harzer Roller (smells terrible, tastes fine). Afterwards she and Magdalena have coffee and cake in a café and pay separately.
lessons.setting: Weekly market, supermarket and Café Eck
grammarFocus: Akkusativ with definite and indefinite articles

items.context: At the market stall Nasrin points to the apples.
items.promptEn: I would like a kilo of apples, please.
items.answerDe: Ich möchte ein Kilo Äpfel, bitte.
items.rule: 'Ich möchte' (I would like) is the polite way to order or ask for something. Quantities go directly before the noun with no 'of': ein Kilo Äpfel, ein Liter Milch, ein Stück Kuchen.
alternativeAnswers: Ich hätte gern ein Kilo Äpfel, bitte.
Ein Kilo Äpfel, bitte.

items.context: Nasrin tells Jamal on the phone what she is buying for dinner.
items.promptEn: I'm buying a salad and a bread.
items.answerDe: Ich kaufe einen Salat und ein Brot.
items.rule: 'kaufen' takes a direct object in the Accusative. 'der Salat' is masculine, so 'ein' becomes 'einen'; 'das Brot' is neuter and stays 'ein'. Only the masculine article changes in the Accusative.

items.context: The market seller hands her the apples and asks: 'Sonst noch etwas?'
items.promptEn: No, thank you. That's all. How much is it?
items.answerDe: Nein, danke. Das ist alles. Was kostet das?
items.rule: 'Was kostet das?' (literally 'what costs that?') is the standard price question; 'Wie viel kostet das?' also works. 'Das ist alles' closes the order.
alternativeAnswers: Nein, danke. Das ist alles. Wie viel kostet das?
Nein, danke. Das wär's. Was kostet das?

items.context: In the café the waiter asks Nasrin: 'Was möchten Sie?'
items.promptEn: I'll take a coffee and a piece of apple cake.
items.answerDe: Ich nehme einen Kaffee und ein Stück Apfelkuchen.
items.rule: 'nehmen' is the normal verb for ordering. It changes its vowel in du/er (du nimmst, er nimmt) but not in 'ich nehme'. 'der Kaffee' is masculine, so Accusative 'einen Kaffee'; 'ein Stück' is neuter and stays 'ein'.
alternativeAnswers: Ich möchte einen Kaffee und ein Stück Apfelkuchen.
Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee und ein Stück Apfelkuchen.

items.context: Nasrin is inviting Magdalena for dinner and needs to know her diet.
items.promptEn: Do you eat meat? (informal)
items.answerDe: Isst du Fleisch?
items.rule: 'essen' changes e to i in the du- and er-forms: du isst, er isst (spelled with -ss- because the vowel is short). Uncountable food like 'Fleisch', 'Brot', 'Milch' takes no article when you mean it in general.

items.context: For her blog Nasrin tastes Harzer Roller and pulls a face.
items.promptEn: I don't like cheese.
items.answerDe: Ich mag keinen Käse.
items.rule: 'mögen' expresses liking a thing directly (no 'gern' needed): ich mag, du magst, er mag – note the ich-form has no ending, like a modal verb. 'Käse' is masculine, so the negative article is Accusative 'keinen'.
alternativeAnswers: Ich mag Käse nicht.

items.context: Nasrin writes the shopping list with Mina.
items.promptEn: We need eggs, tomatoes and potatoes.
items.answerDe: Wir brauchen Eier, Tomaten und Kartoffeln.
items.rule: There is no plural indefinite article in German – 'some eggs' is just 'Eier'. Plurals must be learned with each noun: das Ei → Eier, die Tomate → Tomaten, die Kartoffel → Kartoffeln. 'brauchen' takes the Accusative, but plural nouns without article show no change.

items.context: Nasrin and Magdalena have finished their cake and want to leave.
items.promptEn: The bill, please.
items.answerDe: Die Rechnung, bitte.
items.rule: 'die Rechnung' is the bill. Germans also very often just say 'Zahlen, bitte!' (to pay, please) or 'Wir möchten zahlen'. In a café you usually pay the waiter at the table, not at the counter.
alternativeAnswers: Zahlen, bitte.
Wir möchten zahlen, bitte.
Wir möchten bitte zahlen.

items.context: The waiter comes with the card reader and asks: 'Zusammen oder getrennt?'
items.promptEn: Separately, please.
items.answerDe: Getrennt, bitte.
items.rule: In Germany it is completely normal for friends to pay separately, and waiters ask 'zusammen oder getrennt?' (together or separately) as a matter of routine. 'getrennt' is the participle of 'trennen' (to separate) used as an adverb.
alternativeAnswers: Getrennt bitte.

items.context: Nasrin ends her food-tasting video the way Germans start every meal.
items.promptEn: Enjoy your meal!
items.answerDe: Guten Appetit!
items.rule: 'Guten Appetit' is short for 'Ich wünsche dir/Ihnen einen guten Appetit', which is why 'gut' carries the masculine Accusative ending -en. Germans say it before almost every shared meal; the reply is 'Danke, gleichfalls' (thanks, likewise).

lessons.storyArc: A typical weekday in the Fani household: Nasrin gets up at six, takes Arian to the Kita and Mina to school, sits in class until one, does the housework and picks Arian up in the afternoon. In the evening she practises her new hobby, the flute – badly. She phones the Kita to arrange a parents' meeting and makes a gym date with Magdalena for Saturday.
lessons.setting: The Fani flat, on the phone, on the way to Kita and school
grammarFocus: Separable verbs in the present (aufstehen, abholen, anfangen)
Clock times (um halb vier, um neun Uhr)
Time adverbs (am Nachmittag, abends, sonntags, immer, oft, manchmal, nie)
vocabField: times of day and clock time

items.context: Nasrin describes her morning to the class.
items.promptEn: I get up at six o'clock.
items.answerDe: Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf.
items.rule: 'aufstehen' is a separable verb: in a main clause the prefix 'auf' splits off and goes to the very end of the sentence, while the stem 'stehe' stays in second position. 'um' + clock time = at.
alternativeAnswers: Ich stehe um sechs auf.
Ich stehe um 6 Uhr auf.

items.context: Nasrin has no watch and asks a woman at the bus stop.
items.promptEn: What time is it?
items.answerDe: Wie spät ist es?
items.rule: Literally 'How late is it?' – this is the most common way to ask the time. 'Wie viel Uhr ist es?' is the alternative. Answer with 'Es ist ...'.
alternativeAnswers: Wie viel Uhr ist es?
Entschuldigung, wie spät ist es?

items.context: Nasrin explains her afternoon to Frau Lehmann.
items.promptEn: In the afternoon I pick up Arian from the Kita.
items.answerDe: Am Nachmittag hole ich Arian von der Kita ab.
items.rule: When a time expression starts the sentence, the verb must still be in second position, so the subject moves after it (inversion: Am Nachmittag HOLE ICH ...). The separable prefix 'ab' still goes to the end.
alternativeAnswers: Nachmittags hole ich Arian von der Kita ab.
Am Nachmittag hole ich Arian aus der Kita ab.

items.context: Nasrin calls the Kita for a parents' talk. The employee asks: 'Wann haben Sie Zeit?'
items.promptEn: On Wednesday at half past three?
items.answerDe: Am Mittwoch um halb vier?
items.rule: Careful: 'halb vier' means 3:30, i.e. half of the way TO four, not half past four. Days take 'am' (am Mittwoch), clock times take 'um'.
alternativeAnswers: Mittwoch um halb vier?
Am Mittwoch um 15:30 Uhr?
Am Mittwoch um fünfzehn Uhr dreißig?

items.context: Jamal wants to know when he can call Nasrin during the day.
items.promptEn: The course starts at nine and ends at one.
items.answerDe: Der Kurs beginnt um neun und endet um eins.
items.rule: When the hour stands alone you say 'eins', but with 'Uhr' it is 'ein Uhr' (um ein Uhr). 'beginnen' and 'enden' are regular; 'anfangen' (separable) is the more colloquial alternative for 'to start'.
alternativeAnswers: Der Kurs fängt um neun an und endet um eins.
Der Kurs beginnt um neun Uhr und endet um ein Uhr.

items.context: Nasrin tells Melek about Mina's evening habit.
items.promptEn: Mina reads a book every evening.
items.answerDe: Mina liest jeden Abend ein Buch.
items.rule: 'lesen' changes e to ie in the du- and er/sie-forms: du liest, sie liest. Time expressions like 'jeden Abend', 'jeden Tag' are in the Accusative (der Abend → jeden Abend) and come before the object.
alternativeAnswers: Jeden Abend liest Mina ein Buch.

items.context: Nasrin wants to arrange something with Magdalena after class.
items.promptEn: Do you have time on Saturday? (informal)
items.answerDe: Hast du am Samstag Zeit?
items.rule: 'Zeit haben' = to have time / be free. 'du' with 'haben' is irregular: 'hast'. Days of the week take 'am' (an dem).
alternativeAnswers: Hast du Samstag Zeit?

items.context: Magdalena suggests: 'Gehen wir am Samstag um zehn ins Fitnessstudio?'
items.promptEn: Yes, gladly. See you Saturday then!
items.answerDe: Ja, gern. Bis Samstag dann!
items.rule: 'gern' (or 'gerne') is the standard way to accept an invitation warmly. 'dann' at the end signals that the plan is settled. 'Bis Samstag' = see you (on) Saturday.
alternativeAnswers: Ja, gerne. Bis Samstag dann!
Ja, gern. Bis Samstag!

items.context: In her video blog Nasrin shows her new hobby.
items.promptEn: In the evening I play the flute.
items.answerDe: Abends spiele ich Flöte.
items.rule: Musical instruments take no article with 'spielen': Flöte spielen, Gitarre spielen, Klavier spielen. 'abends' (lowercase, with -s) means 'in the evenings, habitually'. As it starts the sentence, the verb comes next and the subject follows.
alternativeAnswers: Am Abend spiele ich Flöte.
Ich spiele abends Flöte.

items.context: Frau Lehmann asks what the students do on Sundays.
items.promptEn: On Sundays I sleep in (sleep long).
items.answerDe: Sonntags schlafe ich lange.
items.rule: 'sonntags' with -s and lowercase means 'every Sunday' (habit); 'am Sonntag' means one specific Sunday. 'schlafen' changes a to ä only in du/er (du schläfst, er schläft), so 'ich schlafe' is regular. 'lange' = for a long time.
alternativeAnswers: Am Sonntag schlafe ich lange.
Ich schlafe sonntags lange.

lessons.storyArc: The family's flat is too small. Nasrin reads housing ads, phones the landlord Herr Schneider and views a top-floor flat with a balcony and – thankfully – a lift. They get it! The kitchen has a stove, a fridge and a table with four chairs, the bathroom has a bathtub but no shower, and the children get a bunk bed. Nasrin is thrilled about the balcony.
lessons.setting: Apartment viewing and moving day, Hamburg-Eimsbüttel

items.context: Nasrin calls Herr Schneider about the advertisement.
items.promptEn: We are looking for a flat with three rooms.
items.answerDe: Wir suchen eine Wohnung mit drei Zimmern.
items.rule: 'suchen' takes the Accusative: 'eine Wohnung' (feminine, unchanged). 'mit' always takes the Dative, and plural nouns add -n in the Dative: Zimmer → Zimmern. Learn 'mit drei Zimmern' as a fixed phrase – it appears in every housing ad.
alternativeAnswers: Wir suchen eine Dreizimmerwohnung.
Wir suchen eine 3-Zimmer-Wohnung.

items.context: At the viewing Herr Schneider asks: 'Wie viele Personen sind Sie?'
items.promptEn: We are four people: my husband, our two children and I.
items.answerDe: Wir sind vier Personen: mein Mann, unsere zwei Kinder und ich.
items.rule: 'unser' is the possessive for 'wir'. It takes -e before plural nouns (unsere Kinder) and feminine nouns, and no ending before masculine/neuter (unser Sohn). Germans list themselves last: '... und ich'.
alternativeAnswers: Wir sind zu viert: mein Mann, unsere zwei Kinder und ich.

items.context: Nasrin describes the kitchen to Jamal, who couldn't come to the viewing.
items.promptEn: The kitchen is small, but it is bright.
items.answerDe: Die Küche ist klein, aber sie ist hell.
items.rule: German pronouns follow grammatical gender, not whether something is alive. 'die Küche' is feminine, so 'it' must be 'sie'. 'der Balkon' would be 'er' and 'das Bad' would be 'es'.

items.context: The most important question at the viewing.
items.promptEn: How much is the rent?
items.answerDe: Wie hoch ist die Miete?
items.rule: Germans ask 'how HIGH is the rent', not 'how much'. Follow-up vocabulary: 'kalt' (without heating costs) vs. 'warm' (including); 'die Kaution' is the deposit.
alternativeAnswers: Was kostet die Miete?
Wie viel kostet die Miete?
Wie viel ist die Miete?

items.context: Nasrin proudly tells Melek about the new flat.
items.promptEn: Our flat has a balcony.
items.answerDe: Unsere Wohnung hat einen Balkon.
items.rule: 'Wohnung' is feminine, so 'unser' takes -e. 'haben' needs the Accusative, and 'der Balkon' is masculine, so 'ein' becomes 'einen'. Two endings in one short sentence – the classic A1 test sentence.

items.context: Nasrin explains the bathroom to Mina, who loves showers.
items.promptEn: The bathroom has no shower, but a bathtub.
items.answerDe: Das Bad hat keine Dusche, aber eine Badewanne.
items.rule: Both 'Dusche' and 'Badewanne' are feminine, so in the Accusative they keep 'keine' / 'eine'. 'Badewanne' is a compound of baden + Wanne; the last part decides the gender (die Wanne → die Badewanne).
alternativeAnswers: Das Badezimmer hat keine Dusche, aber eine Badewanne.

items.context: Jamal asks where their old wardrobe should go. Nasrin has already decided.
items.promptEn: The wardrobe is old. It stands in the bedroom.
items.answerDe: Der Kleiderschrank ist alt. Er steht im Schlafzimmer.
items.rule: 'der Kleiderschrank' is masculine, so 'it' becomes 'er'. German prefers 'stehen' (to stand) over 'sein' for upright furniture. 'im' is the contraction of 'in dem' – a fixed form you can memorise now; the Dative behind it comes in lesson 7.
alternativeAnswers: Der Kleiderschrank ist alt. Er ist im Schlafzimmer.

items.context: The flat is in the attic floor. Herr Schneider asks: 'Haben Sie noch Fragen?'
items.promptEn: Yes, is there a lift?
items.answerDe: Ja, gibt es einen Aufzug?
items.rule: 'es gibt' (there is/are) is always followed by the Accusative: 'der Aufzug' → 'einen Aufzug'. In a Yes/No question 'gibt' moves to the front and 'es' follows it.
alternativeAnswers: Ja, gibt es einen Fahrstuhl?
Ja, gibt es hier einen Aufzug?

items.context: Saturday cleaning in the new flat. Nasrin explains the division of labour in her blog.
items.promptEn: Jamal cleans the kitchen and I vacuum.
items.answerDe: Jamal putzt die Küche und ich sauge Staub.
items.rule: 'putzen' is the everyday word for cleaning surfaces and rooms. 'Staub saugen' literally means 'to suck dust' – the noun 'Staub' behaves like a separable prefix and goes to the end. 'die Küche' is a feminine Accusative object, so the article stays 'die'.
alternativeAnswers: Jamal putzt die Küche und ich staubsauge.

items.context: Nasrin tells the class where the new flat is in the building.
items.promptEn: The flat is on the top floor (attic floor).
items.answerDe: Die Wohnung ist im Dachgeschoss.
items.rule: 'im' = 'in dem'. 'Dachgeschoss' is a compound: Dach (roof) + Geschoss (storey). Note the floor system: 'Erdgeschoss' is the ground floor, so 'der erste Stock' is the floor above it (US second floor).
alternativeAnswers: Die Wohnung liegt im Dachgeschoss.
Unsere Wohnung ist im Dachgeschoss.

lessons.storyArc: The new flat is in a different district, so Nasrin has to learn new routes: bus line 5 to the U-Bahn, then two stops to the course. She buys a monthly ticket, asks a passer-by the way to the post office and later gives Rafael directions herself. She discovers her favourite place – the park, where she sits on a bench and watches the birds while Arian conquers the playground.
lessons.setting: Streets, bus stop and park in Hamburg
grammarFocus: Dativ after mit, bei, zu, nach (dem/der, zum/zur/beim)
Wechselpräpositionen with Dativ for location (in, an, auf, neben)
vocabField: places and buildings in the city

items.context: Nasrin's first day on the new route. She stops a man on the street.
items.promptEn: Excuse me, how do I get to the train station?
items.answerDe: Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zum Bahnhof?
items.rule: 'Wie komme ich zu ...?' is THE sentence for asking directions. 'zu' always takes the Dative; with masculine/neuter nouns 'zu dem' contracts to 'zum' (der Bahnhof → zum Bahnhof), with feminine nouns 'zu der' becomes 'zur' (zur Post).
alternativeAnswers: Entschuldigen Sie, wie komme ich zum Bahnhof?

items.context: Frau Lehmann asks how everyone gets to class.
items.promptEn: I go by bus to the course.
items.answerDe: Ich fahre mit dem Bus zum Kurs.
items.rule: 'mit' always triggers the Dative: 'der Bus' → 'mit dem Bus'. German uses 'fahren' for any travel with wheels; 'gehen' is only for walking. 'zum Kurs' = zu dem Kurs.

items.context: Rafael is lost near Nasrin's new flat and asks her: 'Wo ist die Post?'
items.promptEn: Go straight ahead, then the first street on the right. (informal)
items.answerDe: Geh geradeaus, dann die erste Straße rechts.
items.rule: The du-imperative is the verb stem without a pronoun and without the -st ending: du gehst → Geh! Direction words 'geradeaus', 'links', 'rechts' need no preposition. 'die erste Straße' is a set direction phrase.
alternativeAnswers: Geh geradeaus und dann die erste Straße rechts.
Geh geradeaus, dann die erste Straße nach rechts.

items.context: Nasrin explains to Rafael exactly where the post office is.
items.promptEn: The post office is next to the bank.
items.answerDe: Die Post ist neben der Bank.
items.rule: 'neben' is a two-way preposition (Wechselpräposition). When you describe WHERE something is (no movement), it takes the Dative: 'die Bank' → 'neben der Bank'. Fun fact: 'die Bank' means both bank and bench.

items.context: Jamal calls and asks where Mina is.
items.promptEn: Mina is at the doctor's.
items.answerDe: Mina ist beim Arzt.
items.rule: 'bei' expresses being at a person's place or business (at the doctor's, at a friend's, at work). It always takes the Dative: 'der Arzt' → 'bei dem Arzt', contracted to 'beim Arzt'.

items.context: Nasrin gets off the U-Bahn and needs the connecting bus.
items.promptEn: Where is the nearest bus stop?
items.answerDe: Wo ist die nächste Haltestelle?
items.rule: 'die Haltestelle' is any bus or tram stop (halten = to stop, Stelle = place). 'nächste' = nearest/next. After 'die' the adjective takes the ending -e in the Nominative.
alternativeAnswers: Wo ist die nächste Bushaltestelle?
Entschuldigung, wo ist die nächste Haltestelle?

items.context: At the HVV service counter the clerk asks: 'Was darf es sein?'
items.promptEn: A monthly ticket, please.
items.answerDe: Eine Monatskarte, bitte.
items.rule: 'die Monatskarte' (month + card) is the season ticket. Compound nouns take the gender of the LAST part: die Karte → die Monatskarte. You can buy things with just noun + 'bitte' – no verb needed.
alternativeAnswers: Ein Monatsticket, bitte.
Ich möchte eine Monatskarte, bitte.
Ich hätte gern eine Monatskarte.

items.context: An elderly woman asks Nasrin the way to the pharmacy. Nasrin answers politely.
items.promptEn: Turn right at the traffic light. (formal)
items.answerDe: Biegen Sie an der Ampel rechts ab.
items.rule: The Sie-imperative is verb + Sie, like a question without the question intonation. 'abbiegen' is separable, so 'ab' goes to the very end. 'an der Ampel' is a location, so 'an' takes the Dative (die Ampel → der Ampel).
alternativeAnswers: Biegen Sie an der Ampel nach rechts ab.
An der Ampel biegen Sie rechts ab.

items.context: It's late. Nasrin leaves the park with Arian.
items.promptEn: I'm going home now.
items.answerDe: Ich gehe jetzt nach Hause.
items.rule: Two fixed phrases you must not mix up: 'nach Hause' = (going) home, direction; 'zu Hause' = at home, location. The -e on 'Hause' is an old Dative ending that survives only in these expressions.
alternativeAnswers: Jetzt gehe ich nach Hause.

items.context: In her blog Nasrin shows her favourite place in the city.
items.promptEn: I am sitting in the park on a bench.
items.answerDe: Ich sitze im Park auf einer Bank.
items.rule: Both prepositions describe a location, so both take the Dative: 'in dem Park' → 'im Park', and 'die Bank' → 'auf einer Bank'. Feminine Dative articles end in -r: der/einer/meiner.
alternativeAnswers: Ich sitze auf einer Bank im Park.

lessons.storyArc: Nasrin has an appointment with Frau Nowak at the Jobcenter. She explains that she worked as a seamstress in Herat for eight years and wants to work in her trade again, but first has to finish her German course. Jamal already works as a car mechanic in a garage. At home Mina announces a new dream job every day – zookeeper, cook, taxi driver, astronaut.
lessons.setting: Jobcenter Hamburg, Frau Nowak's office; the Fani kitchen
grammarFocus: Sentence bracket: modal in position 2, infinitive at the end

items.context: Frau Nowak opens the conversation: 'Was sind Sie von Beruf?'
items.promptEn: I am a seamstress by profession.
items.answerDe: Ich bin Schneiderin von Beruf.
items.rule: Professions take NO article in German: 'Ich bin Schneiderin', not 'eine Schneiderin'. Female job titles add -in (der Schneider → die Schneiderin). 'von Beruf' = by profession.
alternativeAnswers: Ich bin von Beruf Schneiderin.
Ich bin Schneiderin.

items.context: Frau Nowak asks about Nasrin's skills.
items.promptEn: I can sew very well.
items.answerDe: Ich kann sehr gut nähen.
items.rule: Modal verbs form a bracket: the modal ('kann') sits in position 2 and the infinitive ('nähen') goes to the very end. Everything else fits between. In the singular, 'können' loses its umlaut: ich kann, du kannst, er kann.

items.context: Frau Nowak: 'Was möchten Sie in Deutschland machen?'
items.promptEn: I would like to work as a seamstress again.
items.answerDe: Ich möchte wieder als Schneiderin arbeiten.
items.rule: 'möchte' is the polite wish form of 'mögen' and behaves like a modal: infinitive at the end. 'als' + profession (no article) means 'as a ...'. 'wieder' = again.
alternativeAnswers: Ich möchte gern wieder als Schneiderin arbeiten.

items.context: Frau Nowak asks about the family's income.
items.promptEn: My husband works as a car mechanic in a garage.
items.answerDe: Mein Mann arbeitet als Automechaniker in einer Werkstatt.
items.rule: 'arbeiten als' + profession, no article. 'arbeiten' adds an extra -e- in the er-form (arbeit-e-t) because the stem ends in -t. 'in einer Werkstatt' is a location, so 'in' takes the Dative (eine → einer).
alternativeAnswers: Mein Mann arbeitet als Kfz-Mechaniker in einer Werkstatt.
Mein Mann arbeitet als Automechaniker in einer Autowerkstatt.

items.context: Frau Nowak asks when Nasrin could start. Nasrin explains her priority.
items.promptEn: I have to learn German first.
items.answerDe: Ich muss zuerst Deutsch lernen.
items.rule: 'müssen' expresses necessity. Like all modals it loses the umlaut in the singular (ich muss, du musst, er muss) and sends the main verb ('lernen') to the end. 'zuerst' = first (of all).
alternativeAnswers: Zuerst muss ich Deutsch lernen.

items.context: Nasrin reads a job ad for a bakery and calls to ask about the hours.
items.promptEn: When does the work start?
items.answerDe: Wann fängt die Arbeit an?
items.rule: 'anfangen' is separable AND vowel-changing: er/sie/es fängt ... an. In questions too, the prefix 'an' goes to the end. 'Wann' asks about time (when), while 'wenn' means 'if/whenever'.
alternativeAnswers: Wann beginnt die Arbeit?

items.context: Role play in class: Nasrin plays the employer and questions Yonas.
items.promptEn: Can you work at the weekend? (formal)
items.answerDe: Können Sie am Wochenende arbeiten?
items.rule: In a Yes/No question the modal moves to position 1 and the infinitive stays at the very end – the bracket is still there. 'am Wochenende' = at the weekend (an + dem).

items.context: Frau Nowak: 'Haben Sie Berufserfahrung?'
items.promptEn: Yes, I have eight years of work experience.
items.answerDe: Ja, ich habe acht Jahre Berufserfahrung.
items.rule: Durations stand directly before the noun with no preposition: 'acht Jahre Berufserfahrung'. 'Berufserfahrung' (Beruf + s + Erfahrung) is feminine and uncountable, so no article is needed after 'haben'.
alternativeAnswers: Ja, ich habe acht Jahre Erfahrung.

items.context: In her blog Nasrin lists Mina's dream jobs. Today's favourite:
items.promptEn: Mina would like to become a zookeeper.
items.answerDe: Mina möchte Tierpflegerin werden.
items.rule: 'werden' means 'to become' and is used for future professions. Again, no article before the profession. 'möchte' + infinitive 'werden' at the end forms the bracket.
alternativeAnswers: Mina möchte gern Tierpflegerin werden.

items.context: Nasrin summarises what she wants from Frau Nowak.
items.promptEn: I'm looking for a part-time job.
items.answerDe: Ich suche einen Teilzeitjob.
items.rule: 'suchen' takes the Accusative: 'der Job' → 'einen Teilzeitjob'. Useful contrast: Teilzeit (part-time) vs. Vollzeit (full-time) vs. Minijob (up to the tax-free limit).
alternativeAnswers: Ich suche eine Teilzeitstelle.
Ich suche eine Stelle in Teilzeit.

lessons.storyArc: Arian wakes up with a fever and earache. Nasrin phones the paediatric practice, gets an emergency appointment with Dr. Weber and describes his symptoms in German for the first time. The doctor prescribes ear drops and says Arian has to stay home for three days and may not go to the Kita. To cheer him up, Nasrin sings the body-parts song from class.
lessons.setting: Kinderarztpraxis Dr. Weber, and home

items.context: Nasrin explains to the receptionist why she needs an appointment today.
items.promptEn: My son has a fever and earache.
items.answerDe: Mein Sohn hat Fieber und Ohrenschmerzen.
items.rule: 'Fieber haben' takes no article. Pains are compounds ending in the plural '-schmerzen': Ohrenschmerzen, Kopfschmerzen, Bauchschmerzen – always plural, always without article after 'haben'.

items.context: The receptionist picks up: 'Kinderarztpraxis Dr. Weber, guten Tag.'
items.promptEn: Good morning, my name is Fani. I need an appointment for today, please.
items.answerDe: Guten Morgen, mein Name ist Fani. Ich brauche bitte einen Termin für heute.
items.rule: 'einen Termin' – 'der Termin' is masculine and 'brauchen' takes the Accusative. 'Ich brauche einen Termin' may be the single most useful sentence in German bureaucracy. On the phone Germans state their surname first.
alternativeAnswers: Guten Morgen, Fani hier. Ich brauche einen Termin für heute, bitte.
Guten Morgen, mein Name ist Fani. Ich brauche einen Termin für heute.

items.context: Dr. Weber hands Nasrin the ear drops. Nasrin checks the instructions.
items.promptEn: Should he take the drops three times a day?
items.answerDe: Soll er die Tropfen dreimal am Tag nehmen?
items.rule: 'sollen' is used for instructions coming from someone else (the doctor's orders). Like other modals it sends 'nehmen' to the end. 'dreimal am Tag' = three times a day; number + '-mal' forms 'times'.
alternativeAnswers: Soll er die Tropfen dreimal täglich nehmen?

items.context: Arian is crying. Nasrin tries to find out what's wrong.
items.promptEn: Where does it hurt?
items.answerDe: Wo tut es weh?
items.rule: 'wehtun' (to hurt) is separable: 'tut ... weh'. The thing that hurts is the subject and the person is in the Dative: 'Mein Ohr tut mir weh'. With the dummy subject 'es' you get the general question 'Wo tut es weh?'.
alternativeAnswers: Wo tut es dir weh?
Wo tut's weh?

items.context: Nasrin phones Jamal after the appointment to pass on the doctor's decision.
items.promptEn: He is not allowed to go to the Kita.
items.answerDe: Er darf nicht in die Kita gehen.
items.rule: 'dürfen' = to be allowed to; 'nicht dürfen' = must not / not allowed. Singular forms drop the umlaut: ich darf, du darfst, er darf. 'in die Kita' is a direction (going INTO), so 'in' takes the Accusative here.

items.context: Dr. Weber examines Arian and asks: 'Seit wann hat er Fieber?'
items.promptEn: Since yesterday evening.
items.answerDe: Seit gestern Abend.
items.rule: 'seit' (since/for) answers 'Seit wann?'. 'gestern Abend' combines a lowercase adverb (gestern) with a capitalised noun (Abend). Same pattern: heute Morgen, morgen früh.
alternativeAnswers: Seit gestern Abend hat er Fieber.
Er hat seit gestern Abend Fieber.

items.context: Back home, Nasrin doesn't want Mina to catch the bug. She calls both children to the sink.
items.promptEn: Children, wash your hands! (to both kids)
items.answerDe: Kinder, wascht eure Hände!
items.rule: The ihr-imperative is simply the ihr-form of the verb without the pronoun: ihr wascht → Wascht! The possessive for 'ihr' is 'euer'; before a plural or feminine noun it becomes 'eure' (the second e of 'euer' drops out).
alternativeAnswers: Kinder, wascht euch die Hände!

items.context: Melek hears Arian is sick and writes to Nasrin. Nasrin later uses the same phrase for Frau Lehmann, who has a cold.
items.promptEn: Get well soon!
items.answerDe: Gute Besserung!
items.rule: Literally 'good improvement'. It is short for 'Ich wünsche dir/Ihnen gute Besserung', which is why it is in the Accusative – but since 'Besserung' is feminine, the ending -e looks the same as the Nominative.

items.context: A few days later Nasrin has caught Arian's virus and tells Frau Lehmann why she looks tired.
items.promptEn: I have a headache and a sore throat.
items.answerDe: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen und Halsschmerzen.
items.rule: Where English says 'a headache', German uses the plural compound 'Kopfschmerzen' with no article. Sore throat = 'Halsschmerzen' (Hals = neck/throat). You can shorten the pair to 'Kopf- und Halsschmerzen'.
alternativeAnswers: Ich habe Kopf- und Halsschmerzen.

items.context: Before leaving the practice, Nasrin remembers the Kita's rules.
items.promptEn: I need a doctor's certificate for the Kita.
items.answerDe: Ich brauche ein Attest für die Kita.
items.rule: 'das Attest' is the doctor's certificate confirming illness (for work it is called 'die Krankschreibung' or 'Krankmeldung'). 'für' always takes the Accusative; 'die Kita' is feminine, so the article does not change.
alternativeAnswers: Ich brauche eine Bescheinigung für die Kita.

lessons.storyArc: Monday morning – everyone in class talks about the weekend. Nasrin tells about her stressful Saturday: Melek called in the morning and wanted to visit in the afternoon, so Nasrin tidied up, cleaned, baked a cake, picked up the kids and missed the bus twice. On Sunday the family did a boat trip on the Alster and she slept better than she had in ages.
lessons.setting: Classroom, Monday morning
grammarFocus: Partizip II: weak (gemacht), strong (gebacken), -ieren (telefoniert), separable (aufgeräumt), inseparable (verpasst)
Time expressions: gestern, letzte Woche, heute Morgen

items.context: Frau Lehmann asks Nasrin what she did on Saturday.
items.promptEn: Yesterday I baked a cake. (use Perfekt)
items.answerDe: Gestern habe ich einen Kuchen gebacken.
items.rule: The Perfekt is a bracket: 'haben' in position 2, the Partizip II at the very end. 'backen' is a strong verb, so its participle is 'ge-back-en' (not -t). 'Gestern' in first position pushes the subject behind the verb.
alternativeAnswers: Ich habe gestern einen Kuchen gebacken.

items.context: Nasrin sums up her weekend in one sentence.
items.promptEn: The weekend was very stressful.
items.answerDe: Das Wochenende war sehr stressig.
items.rule: For 'sein' and 'haben', Germans use the simple past (Präteritum) even in speech: 'war', not 'ist gewesen'. Forms: ich war, du warst, er war, wir waren. 'stressig' after 'sein' takes no ending.

items.context: Frau Lehmann: 'Was haben Sie am Wochenende gemacht, Frau Fani?'
items.promptEn: I tidied up and cleaned.
items.answerDe: Ich habe aufgeräumt und geputzt.
items.rule: Weak verbs form the participle with ge- + stem + -t: putzen → geputzt. With separable verbs the 'ge' squeezes BETWEEN prefix and stem: auf-ge-räumt. One 'habe' can serve two participles.
alternativeAnswers: Ich habe aufgeräumt und sauber gemacht.

items.context: Nasrin describes the moment her friend arrived.
items.promptEn: Melek came at three o'clock. (use Perfekt)
items.answerDe: Melek ist um drei Uhr gekommen.
items.rule: Verbs of movement from A to B (kommen, gehen, fahren, fliegen) and change of state form the Perfekt with 'sein', not 'haben'. 'kommen' is strong: 'gekommen'.
alternativeAnswers: Melek ist um drei gekommen.
Um drei Uhr ist Melek gekommen.

items.context: Nasrin explains why she was late picking up the children.
items.promptEn: I missed the bus twice.
items.answerDe: Ich habe zweimal den Bus verpasst.
items.rule: Verbs with inseparable prefixes (ver-, be-, er-, ent-) form the participle WITHOUT 'ge': verpassen → verpasst. 'den Bus' is masculine Accusative. 'zweimal' = twice.
alternativeAnswers: Ich habe den Bus zweimal verpasst.

items.context: Rafael asks why Nasrin didn't answer his message on Saturday.
items.promptEn: Yesterday I had no time.
items.answerDe: Gestern hatte ich keine Zeit.
items.rule: 'hatte' is the Präteritum of 'haben' – like 'war', it is preferred over the Perfekt in spoken German. 'keine Zeit' is a feminine Accusative object. Inversion after 'Gestern'.
alternativeAnswers: Ich hatte gestern keine Zeit.

items.context: Nasrin also mentions what she did on Sunday evening.
items.promptEn: I phoned my mother. (use 'telefonieren')
items.answerDe: Ich habe mit meiner Mutter telefoniert.
items.rule: Verbs ending in -ieren never take 'ge-': telefonieren → telefoniert. 'telefonieren mit' requires the Dative: 'meine Mutter' → 'mit meiner Mutter' (feminine Dative ends in -er).

items.context: Rafael is curious: 'Und, wie war der Besuch?'
items.promptEn: Great! We ate cake and talked a lot.
items.answerDe: Toll! Wir haben Kuchen gegessen und viel geredet.
items.rule: 'essen' has an unusual participle with a double g: 'gegessen'. 'reden' is weak but the stem ends in -d, so it adds -et: 'geredet'. 'Kuchen' in general takes no article.
alternativeAnswers: Super! Wir haben Kuchen gegessen und viel gesprochen.
Toll! Wir haben Kuchen gegessen und viel gesprochen.

items.context: After the exhausting Saturday, Nasrin enjoyed her Sunday.
items.promptEn: This morning I slept until nine. (use Perfekt)
items.answerDe: Heute Morgen habe ich bis neun geschlafen.
items.rule: 'schlafen' is strong (geschlafen) but takes 'haben', because sleeping is not movement or change of state. 'heute Morgen' = this morning; 'bis neun' = until nine.
alternativeAnswers: Ich habe heute Morgen bis neun geschlafen.
Heute Morgen habe ich bis neun Uhr geschlafen.

items.context: Nasrin mentions the family's short trip the week before.
items.promptEn: Last week we were in Lübeck.
items.answerDe: Letzte Woche waren wir in Lübeck.
items.rule: 'waren' is the wir-form of 'war'. Time expressions like 'letzte Woche', 'letzten Monat', 'letztes Jahr' are in the Accusative without a preposition and typically open the sentence, triggering inversion.
alternativeAnswers: Wir waren letzte Woche in Lübeck.

lessons.storyArc: The children need new clothes, so the family goes to a department store. For Arian, who grows so fast, Nasrin buys a T-shirt, trousers, a jumper, a jacket and rubber boots. Mina hates the skirt and blouse her mother picked out and chooses jeans, a hoodie and trainers herself – at least they both like the coat. Back home the jacket turns out to be too small and Nasrin goes back to exchange it.
lessons.setting: Department store in Hamburg city centre
grammarFocus: Dativ pronouns with gefallen, passen, stehen, helfen
Comparative and superlative (billiger als, am besten)
Demonstrative dies- and question word welch- in Nom/Akk

items.context: A sales assistant approaches Nasrin: 'Kann ich Ihnen helfen?'
items.promptEn: Thanks, I'm just looking.
items.answerDe: Danke, ich schaue nur.
items.rule: This is the standard polite brush-off in any German shop. 'schauen' (to look) is the natural verb here; 'gucken' is the colloquial northern alternative. Note the assistant's 'Ihnen' – 'helfen' takes the Dative.
alternativeAnswers: Danke, ich schaue mich nur um.
Danke, ich gucke nur.

items.context: Arian tries on the jacket at home and can't close it.
items.promptEn: The jacket doesn't fit him.
items.answerDe: Die Jacke passt ihm nicht.
items.rule: 'passen' (to fit) works backwards from English: the item of clothing is the subject and the person is in the Dative. 'er' becomes 'ihm' in the Dative. Same pattern for gefallen, stehen, helfen.

items.context: Mina holds up a coat. For once Nasrin agrees with her.
items.promptEn: I like the coat. (use 'gefallen')
items.answerDe: Der Mantel gefällt mir.
items.rule: 'gefallen' means 'to be pleasing to'. The thing you like is the subject (der Mantel → gefällt, with vowel change a→ä) and YOU are in the Dative: 'mir'. Think 'the coat pleases me'.
alternativeAnswers: Der Mantel gefällt mir gut.

items.context: Nasrin holds two jumpers up for Mina to choose.
items.promptEn: Which jumper are you taking? (informal)
items.answerDe: Welchen Pullover nimmst du?
items.rule: 'welch-' takes the same endings as the definite article. 'der Pullover' is masculine and the direct object of 'nehmen', so it is Accusative: den → welchen. 'nehmen' changes e→i in the du-form: nimmst.
alternativeAnswers: Welchen Pulli nimmst du?

items.context: The sales assistant asks: 'Welche Größe brauchen Sie?'
items.promptEn: Size 128, please. Do you have the jacket in blue?
items.answerDe: Größe 128, bitte. Haben Sie die Jacke in Blau?
items.rule: Children's clothes in Germany are sized by height in cm (128 = about 8 years). After 'in', colours are used as nouns and capitalised: 'in Blau', 'in Rot'. 'die Jacke' is a feminine Accusative object.
alternativeAnswers: Größe 128, bitte. Haben Sie diese Jacke in Blau?
Größe hundertachtundzwanzig, bitte. Haben Sie die Jacke in Blau?

items.context: The next day Nasrin is back at the counter with the too-small jacket.
items.promptEn: I would like to exchange this jacket.
items.answerDe: Ich möchte diese Jacke umtauschen.
items.rule: 'dies-' points at something specific and takes definite-article endings: 'die Jacke' → 'diese Jacke' (feminine, Accusative = Nominative). 'umtauschen' is separable, but after 'möchte' the whole infinitive stays together at the end.
alternativeAnswers: Ich möchte diese Jacke gern umtauschen.
Ich möchte die Jacke umtauschen.

items.context: Nasrin compares prices to convince Mina.
items.promptEn: The jeans are cheaper than the skirt.
items.answerDe: Die Jeans ist billiger als der Rock.
items.rule: The comparative is formed with -er (billig → billiger) and the comparison word is 'als' (than). Unlike English, 'die Jeans' is singular in German, so the verb is 'ist'.
alternativeAnswers: Die Jeans ist günstiger als der Rock.

items.context: Mina is unsure about the blue hoodie. Nasrin encourages her.
items.promptEn: Blue suits you. (informal)
items.answerDe: Blau steht dir gut.
items.rule: 'stehen' + Dativ means 'to suit' someone: 'Das steht dir/Ihnen gut'. The colour is the subject; the person is in the Dative (du → dir). Without 'gut' it still works but sounds less warm.
alternativeAnswers: Blau steht dir.
Blau steht dir sehr gut.

items.context: Mina has tried on three pairs of shoes and gives her verdict – which Nasrin repeats to Jamal.
items.promptEn: She likes the trainers best. (use 'gefallen')
items.answerDe: Die Turnschuhe gefallen ihr am besten.
items.rule: Superlative as an adverb: 'am' + -sten (gut → am besten, irregular). 'die Turnschuhe' is plural and the subject, so the verb is plural 'gefallen'. 'sie' (she) becomes 'ihr' in the Dative.
alternativeAnswers: Ihr gefallen die Turnschuhe am besten.

items.context: Nasrin tells Jamal she won't be shopping alone this time.
items.promptEn: I'm going to the department store with a friend (female).
items.answerDe: Ich gehe mit einer Freundin ins Kaufhaus.
items.rule: 'mit' forces the Dative on the indefinite article: 'eine Freundin' → 'mit einer Freundin'. 'ins' (in das) is Accusative because it is a direction – going INTO the store.
alternativeAnswers: Ich gehe mit einer Freundin in das Kaufhaus.

lessons.storyArc: Winter arrives in Hamburg: it's cold, grey and windy, and then the first snow falls. Nasrin misses the sun of Herat, but Arian discovers sledging. The family fills in the new calendar: Mina's birthday on 14 February, Nasrin's A1 exam on 3 March, Nowruz on 21 March. Nasrin wants to pass the exam – and then, one day, travel through Germany.
lessons.setting: The Fani flat, the park in snow, classroom
grammarFocus: Ordinal numbers and dates (am vierzehnten Februar)

items.context: Nasrin looks out of the window at the grey sky and asks Jamal, who has checked his phone.
items.promptEn: What's the weather like today?
items.answerDe: Wie ist das Wetter heute?
items.rule: German asks 'HOW is the weather', not 'what is the weather like'. 'das Wetter' is neuter. Typical answers: 'Es regnet', 'Es ist kalt', 'Die Sonne scheint'.
alternativeAnswers: Wie ist heute das Wetter?

items.context: Frau Lehmann asks about everyone's goals for the new year.
items.promptEn: I want to pass the A1 exam.
items.answerDe: Ich will die A1-Prüfung bestehen.
items.rule: 'wollen' expresses a firm intention. Singular forms lose the umlaut and 'ich will' has no ending. Warning: German 'will' means 'want', never the English future 'will'. 'bestehen' (to pass) goes to the end.
alternativeAnswers: Ich will die Prüfung A1 bestehen.
Ich will die A1-Prüfung schaffen.

items.context: Nasrin records a short winter update for her blog from the balcony.
items.promptEn: It's cold and it's snowing.
items.answerDe: Es ist kalt und es schneit.
items.rule: Weather verbs need the dummy subject 'es': es schneit, es regnet, es ist kalt. There is no 'it' to leave out – German always needs a subject in position 1 or 3.
alternativeAnswers: Es ist kalt, und es schneit.

items.context: Nasrin writes the family dates into the new calendar and reads them out.
items.promptEn: Mina's birthday is on the 14th of February. (use 'Geburtstag haben')
items.answerDe: Mina hat am vierzehnten Februar Geburtstag.
items.rule: Dates use 'am' + ordinal number. Ordinals 1–19 add -te (vierzehnte), 20 and above add -ste; after 'am' (Dative) they get -n: am vierzehnten. Germans 'have birthday' – 'Geburtstag haben'.
alternativeAnswers: Mina hat am 14. Februar Geburtstag.
Minas Geburtstag ist am vierzehnten Februar.
Minas Geburtstag ist am 14. Februar.

items.context: Filling in the exam registration form, Frau Lehmann asks: 'Wann sind Sie geboren?'
items.promptEn: I was born on the 2nd of May 1992.
items.answerDe: Ich bin am zweiten Mai 1992 geboren.
items.rule: German uses the present tense of 'sein' + 'geboren' for living people: 'Ich bin ... geboren'. Years are said without 'in': 1992 = 'neunzehnhundertzweiundneunzig'. The ordinal after 'am' takes -n: am zweiten.
alternativeAnswers: Ich bin am 2. Mai 1992 geboren.
Ich bin am zweiten Mai neunzehnhundertzweiundneunzig geboren.

items.context: Nasrin explains to Melek what Herat is like compared to Hamburg.
items.promptEn: In summer it is warm and sunny.
items.answerDe: Im Sommer ist es warm und sonnig.
items.rule: Seasons and months take 'im' (in dem): im Sommer, im Winter, im Mai. Starting with the time expression forces inversion: the verb 'ist' comes second and 'es' third.

items.context: First snow! Mina and Arian are already putting on their boots.
items.promptEn: The children want to go sledging.
items.answerDe: Die Kinder wollen Schlitten fahren.
items.rule: Plural 'wollen' keeps the infinitive form. 'Schlitten fahren' (to sledge) is a noun + verb combination like 'Ski fahren' or 'Rad fahren'; the noun is capitalised and the whole unit goes to the end.
alternativeAnswers: Die Kinder wollen rodeln.

items.context: Nasrin opens her blog on the day of the Persian New Year.
items.promptEn: Today is the 21st of March.
items.answerDe: Heute ist der einundzwanzigste März.
items.rule: When the date is the subject, it stands in the Nominative: 'der' + ordinal + -e. From 20 upwards the ordinal ending is -ste (einundzwanzigste). Written with a dot: 'der 21. März'.
alternativeAnswers: Heute ist der 21. März.

items.context: Melek asks: 'Was macht ihr an Nouruz?'
items.promptEn: We celebrate at home with the whole family.
items.answerDe: Wir feiern zu Hause mit der ganzen Familie.
items.rule: 'zu Hause' = at home (location). 'mit' takes the Dative: 'die ganze Familie' → 'mit der ganzen Familie' – feminine Dative article 'der', and the adjective takes -en after it.
alternativeAnswers: Wir feiern mit der ganzen Familie zu Hause.

items.context: Nasrin ends the winter blog on a hopeful note.
items.promptEn: In spring the sun shines again.
items.answerDe: Im Frühling scheint wieder die Sonne.
items.rule: 'die Sonne scheint' = the sun shines/is shining. After the time phrase 'im Frühling' the verb comes second; the subject 'die Sonne' can follow 'wieder' for emphasis or stand right after the verb – both are correct.
alternativeAnswers: Im Frühling scheint die Sonne wieder.

lessons.titleEn: What are we doing at the weekend?
lessons.storyArc: Nasrin has passed her A1 exam and started the A2 course. At Mina's school summer fest she enters a raffle and wins a rail ticket valid all over Germany! She plans a trip through Germany in the autumn holidays, invites Melek to the fest, checks the weather app and finally organises a small celebration for her exam.
lessons.setting: Mina's school fest and the Fani flat, Hamburg
grammarFocus: Personalpronomen Akkusativ (mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch)
Indefinitpronomen ein-/kein- in Akkusativ (Ich habe einen.)

items.context: The Fanis are planning Saturday. Nasrin asks Jamal to look at the weather app.
items.promptEn: What is the weather going to be like at the weekend?
items.answerDe: Wie wird das Wetter am Wochenende?
items.rule: For the future weather Germans use 'werden' (to become): 'Wie wird das Wetter?' = How will the weather turn out? 'wird' is the irregular er/es-form of 'werden'.
alternativeAnswers: Wie wird am Wochenende das Wetter?
Wie soll das Wetter am Wochenende werden?

items.context: Nasrin tells Melek about the school fest and invites her.
items.promptEn: I'm inviting you to the school fest. (informal)
items.answerDe: Ich lade dich zum Schulfest ein.
items.rule: 'einladen' takes a direct object in the Accusative, and 'du' becomes 'dich' in the Accusative. 'einladen' is separable and vowel-changing (er lädt ... ein). 'zum Schulfest' = zu dem Schulfest (Dative after zu).

items.context: Melek hesitates: 'Hmm, am Samstag ... Wann fängt das Fest an?'
items.promptEn: At two. Are you coming? I'll pick you up. (informal)
items.answerDe: Um zwei. Kommst du? Ich hole dich ab.
items.rule: 'abholen' (to pick up) is separable: 'hole ... ab', with the Accusative pronoun 'dich' inside the bracket. German uses the present tense for near-future arrangements – no future tense needed.
alternativeAnswers: Um zwei Uhr. Kommst du? Ich hole dich ab.

items.context: Nasrin comes home from the fest waving a ticket. Jamal asks what one can do with it.
items.promptEn: With this ticket one can travel through all of Germany.
items.answerDe: Mit dieser Fahrkarte kann man durch ganz Deutschland fahren.
items.rule: 'man' is the impersonal 'one/you/people' and always takes the er/sie/es verb form (kann). 'mit dieser Fahrkarte' – 'mit' + Dative, feminine 'diese' becomes 'dieser'. 'durch' takes the Accusative, but 'Deutschland' has no article so nothing shows.
alternativeAnswers: Mit diesem Ticket kann man durch ganz Deutschland fahren.

items.context: Nasrin describes her new city-guide app in her blog.
items.promptEn: With this app one can find all the sights in a city.
items.answerDe: Mit dieser App kann man alle Sehenswürdigkeiten in einer Stadt finden.
items.rule: 'die Sehenswürdigkeit' (sight, literally 'worth-seeing-ness') is plural here: 'alle Sehenswürdigkeiten'. 'man kann ... finden' forms a modal bracket; 'in einer Stadt' is a location (Dative).

items.context: Melek asks whether Nasrin already has a rucksack for the trip.
items.promptEn: No, I don't have one. (referring to 'der Rucksack')
items.answerDe: Nein, ich habe keinen.
items.rule: To avoid repeating the noun, German uses 'ein-/kein-' as a stand-alone pronoun with the full article ending. 'der Rucksack' is masculine and the object of 'haben', so Accusative: 'keinen'. Positive: 'Ja, ich habe einen.'

items.context: Frau Lehmann asks: 'Wie feiern Sie Ihre bestandene Prüfung, Frau Fani?'
items.promptEn: My friends are visiting us on Sunday and we're cooking together.
items.answerDe: Meine Freunde besuchen uns am Sonntag und wir kochen zusammen.
items.rule: 'besuchen' takes the Accusative; 'wir' becomes 'uns'. Note 'am Sonntag' (one specific Sunday) versus 'sonntags' (every Sunday). Two main clauses joined by 'und' each keep verb-second order.
alternativeAnswers: Am Sonntag besuchen uns meine Freunde und wir kochen zusammen.

items.context: It's Rafael's birthday at the fest. Nasrin congratulates him.
items.promptEn: Happy birthday! (literally: all the best for your birthday)
items.answerDe: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!
items.rule: 'Alles Gute' = all good things; 'zum Geburtstag' = for the birthday (zu + dem). This is the universal German birthday wish. The adjective 'Gute' is capitalised because after 'alles' it functions as a noun.
alternativeAnswers: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!

items.context: Jamal has gone to buy drinks for the party. Mina asks where he is.
items.promptEn: I'll call him quickly.
items.answerDe: Ich rufe ihn schnell an.
items.rule: 'anrufen' takes the Accusative (unlike English 'call TO'). 'er' becomes 'ihn' in the Accusative – the only personal pronoun besides 'mich/dich/uns/euch' that visibly changes. Separable prefix 'an' at the end.
alternativeAnswers: Ich rufe ihn kurz an.

items.context: Melek can't come on Sunday after all. Nasrin suggests another time.
items.promptEn: Do you have time next week? (informal)
items.answerDe: Hast du nächste Woche Zeit?
items.rule: 'nächste Woche' (next week) is a time expression in the Accusative without preposition – like 'letzte Woche'. It is feminine, so the adjective ending is -e. 'Zeit haben' = to be free.

lessons.storyArc: The autumn holidays begin and Nasrin sets off on her Germany trip – north to south: Bremen, Köln, Frankfurt, München. At Hamburg Hauptbahnhof she reserves a seat, finds her platform and sends greetings from the train. In Bremen she asks the way to the Bremer Stadtmusikanten and takes a bus to a sweet shop with green-and-white bonbons.
lessons.setting: Hamburg Hauptbahnhof, the train, Bremen city centre
grammarFocus: Review: bei, zu, nach and two-way prepositions with Dativ

items.context: At the DB travel centre the clerk asks: 'Was kann ich für Sie tun?'
items.promptEn: I would like to reserve a seat to Bremen, please.
items.answerDe: Ich möchte bitte einen Sitzplatz nach Bremen reservieren.
items.rule: 'der Sitzplatz' is masculine, so 'einen'. Cities take 'nach' for direction. 'reservieren' is an -ieren verb; its participle would be 'reserviert' without 'ge-'.
alternativeAnswers: Ich möchte einen Sitzplatz nach Bremen reservieren, bitte.
Ich hätte gern eine Sitzplatzreservierung nach Bremen.

items.context: Nasrin looks at the departures board but can't find her train.
items.promptEn: Which platform does the train to Bremen leave from?
items.answerDe: Von welchem Gleis fährt der Zug nach Bremen ab?
items.rule: 'von' takes the Dative, so 'welches Gleis' (neuter) becomes 'welchem Gleis'. 'abfahren' (to depart) is separable; 'ab' goes to the end. Railway platforms are 'Gleis' (track), not 'Plattform'.
alternativeAnswers: Von welchem Gleis fährt der Zug nach Bremen?
Auf welchem Gleis fährt der Zug nach Bremen ab?

items.context: In her blog Nasrin explains why she must visit the Kölner Dom.
items.promptEn: The Cologne Cathedral is the biggest, that's why I have to go in.
items.answerDe: Der Kölner Dom ist am größten, deshalb muss ich da unbedingt rein.
items.rule: 'deshalb' (that's why) counts as position 1, so the verb comes IMMEDIATELY after it: 'deshalb muss ich'. Superlative after 'sein' as adverb: 'am größten'. 'rein' is colloquial for 'hinein'; with a modal the verb of motion can be dropped.
alternativeAnswers: Der Kölner Dom ist am größten, deshalb muss ich unbedingt reingehen.
Der Kölner Dom ist am größten, deshalb muss ich da unbedingt reingehen.

items.context: Nasrin's train stops in the middle of nowhere. She asks the conductor.
items.promptEn: Does the train have a delay?
items.answerDe: Hat der Zug Verspätung?
items.rule: 'Verspätung haben' (to have delay) takes no article. Nasrin will hear the announcement 'Der Zug hat circa 20 Minuten Verspätung' – a phrase every German commuter knows by heart.
alternativeAnswers: Entschuldigung, hat der Zug Verspätung?

items.context: On the train a woman asks whether the seat next to Nasrin is taken. Nasrin points at a bag on the seat.
items.promptEn: Is that your suitcase? – No, that isn't one. That's a bag. (referring to 'der Koffer')
items.answerDe: Ist das Ihr Koffer? – Nein, das ist keiner. Das ist eine Tasche.
items.rule: As a stand-alone pronoun, 'kein-' needs the full article ending even in the Nominative masculine: 'keiner' (compare 'kein Koffer' with the noun). Neuter would be 'keins', feminine 'keine'.

items.context: In Bremen Nasrin stops a passer-by.
items.promptEn: Excuse me, how do I get to the town hall?
items.answerDe: Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zum Rathaus?
items.rule: Review of 'zu' + Dative: 'das Rathaus' (neuter) → 'zu dem' → 'zum'. Compare 'zur Kirche' (feminine). 'nach' is only used for cities, countries and 'nach Hause'.
alternativeAnswers: Entschuldigen Sie, wie komme ich zum Rathaus?

items.context: The passer-by says: 'Das Rathaus? Das ist weit. Gehen Sie zu Fuß?'
items.promptEn: No, I'll take the bus. Which line goes to the town hall?
items.answerDe: Nein, ich nehme den Bus. Welche Linie fährt zum Rathaus?
items.rule: 'den Bus nehmen' = to take the bus (masculine Accusative). 'die Linie' is feminine, so 'welche' in the Nominative. Buses and trains 'fahren', they don't 'gehen'.
alternativeAnswers: Nein, ich fahre mit dem Bus. Welche Linie fährt zum Rathaus?

items.context: Nasrin explains in her blog why she is starting in Bremen.
items.promptEn: My friend Samira lives in Bremen, that's why my first stop is Bremen.
items.answerDe: Meine Freundin Samira wohnt in Bremen, deshalb ist mein erster Halt Bremen.
items.rule: Again 'deshalb' + verb + subject. 'mein erster Halt' – after 'mein' (no ending, masculine Nominative) the adjective takes -er to show the gender: 'erster'. 'der Halt' = stop.
alternativeAnswers: Meine Freundin Samira wohnt in Bremen, deshalb ist Bremen mein erster Halt.

items.context: Nasrin tastes the famous green-and-white bonbons in the sweet shop.
items.promptEn: The green-and-white bonbons are the tastiest.
items.answerDe: Die grün-weißen Bonbons sind am leckersten.
items.rule: Superlative as predicate: 'am' + adjective + '-sten' (lecker → am leckersten). The adjective before the plural noun takes -en after 'die': 'die grün-weißen Bonbons'.
alternativeAnswers: Die grün-weißen Bonbons schmecken am besten.

items.context: The conductor comes through the carriage. Nasrin has her winning ticket ready.
items.promptEn: Here is my ticket. I'm travelling to Bremen and then on to Cologne.
items.answerDe: Hier ist meine Fahrkarte. Ich fahre nach Bremen und dann weiter nach Köln.
items.rule: 'weiterfahren' (to travel on) is separable; here 'weiter' stands before the destination. Cities always take 'nach'. 'die Fahrkarte' is feminine: 'meine'.
alternativeAnswers: Hier ist mein Ticket. Ich fahre nach Bremen und dann weiter nach Köln.

lessons.storyArc: In Bremen Nasrin stays with her friend Samira, who lives with her daughter in a shared house (WG) with a student and an elderly couple – seven rooms, two bathrooms, one cleaning rota. Samira has just moved into a bigger room upstairs, so Nasrin helps: the bed goes against the wall, the lamp on the desk, the picture above the sofa. Whoever ignores the cleaning rota pays five euros into the house kitty.
lessons.setting: Samira's shared house (WG) in Bremen
grammarFocus: Sequence words zuerst, dann, danach, schließlich

items.context: Samira asks where the bed should go. Nasrin has an idea.
items.promptEn: We'll put the bed against the wall. (use 'stellen')
items.answerDe: Wir stellen das Bett an die Wand.
items.rule: 'stellen' describes putting something upright somewhere – a movement toward a goal – so the two-way preposition 'an' takes the Accusative: 'die Wand' stays 'die Wand'. Once it is there, you say 'Das Bett steht an der Wand' (Dative).

items.context: Tim wants to know where the picture ended up.
items.promptEn: The picture is hanging above the sofa.
items.answerDe: Das Bild hängt über dem Sofa.
items.rule: Location, no movement → Dative. 'das Sofa' is neuter, so 'über dem Sofa'. 'hängen' is one verb for both meanings, but the case after the preposition tells you whether it is 'hang up' (Akk) or 'be hanging' (Dat).

items.context: Samira can't find her keys. Nasrin spots them.
items.promptEn: Your keys are lying on the table.
items.answerDe: Deine Schlüssel liegen auf dem Tisch.
items.rule: 'liegen' = to lie (flat), a location verb, so 'auf' takes the Dative: 'der Tisch' → 'auf dem Tisch'. 'Schlüssel' has the same form in singular and plural; the verb 'liegen' shows it is plural here.

items.context: Samira holds up the lamp and asks: 'Und wohin mit der Lampe?'
items.promptEn: Put it on the desk. (informal, use 'stellen')
items.answerDe: Stell sie auf den Schreibtisch.
items.rule: 'Wohin?' (where to) demands the Accusative: 'der Schreibtisch' → 'auf den Schreibtisch'. The du-imperative of 'stellen' is 'Stell'. 'die Lampe' is feminine, so the pronoun is 'sie'.
alternativeAnswers: Stell sie auf den Schreibtisch!
Stell die Lampe auf den Schreibtisch.

items.context: Nasrin explains the WG cleaning rules in her blog.
items.promptEn: A cleaning rota hangs in the kitchen.
items.answerDe: In der Küche hängt ein Putzplan.
items.rule: 'in der Küche' – location, Dative, feminine 'der'. Starting with the place phrase puts the verb second and the subject 'ein Putzplan' after it. 'der Putzplan' (putzen + Plan) is a fixture of every German WG.
alternativeAnswers: Ein Putzplan hängt in der Küche.

items.context: Nasrin describes the moving day step by step.
items.promptEn: First we carried the boxes upstairs, then we set up the bed.
items.answerDe: Zuerst haben wir die Kartons nach oben getragen, dann haben wir das Bett aufgebaut.
items.rule: Sequence words 'zuerst, dann, danach, schließlich' each take position 1, so the verb follows immediately. 'tragen' is strong (getragen), 'aufbauen' is separable-weak (auf-ge-baut). 'nach oben' = upstairs (direction).
alternativeAnswers: Zuerst haben wir die Kisten nach oben getragen, dann haben wir das Bett aufgebaut.

items.context: Nasrin is impressed by the WG's solution to cleaning disputes.
items.promptEn: Whoever doesn't follow the rota has to pay five euros into the house kitty.
items.answerDe: Wer den Putzplan nicht beachtet, muss fünf Euro in die Hauskasse einzahlen.
items.rule: 'Wer ..., (der) ...' is a generalising relative clause: the verb goes to the end of the 'wer' part ('beachtet') and the main clause starts with the verb ('muss'). 'in die Hauskasse' is a direction → Accusative. 'einzahlen' = to pay in.
alternativeAnswers: Wer den Putzplan nicht beachtet, muss fünf Euro in die Hauskasse zahlen.

items.context: Frau Krüger from downstairs knocks: 'Entschuldigung, wer sind Sie denn?'
items.promptEn: Good evening, I'm Nasrin, a friend of Samira's. I'm helping her with the move.
items.answerDe: Guten Abend, ich bin Nasrin, eine Freundin von Samira. Ich helfe ihr beim Umzug.
items.rule: 'helfen' takes the Dative: 'sie' (Samira) → 'ihr'. 'helfen bei' + Dative = to help with; 'bei dem Umzug' contracts to 'beim Umzug'. 'eine Freundin von' + name is the everyday way to say 'a friend of'.
alternativeAnswers: Guten Abend, ich bin Nasrin, Samiras Freundin. Ich helfe ihr beim Umzug.

items.context: Nasrin describes the WG in her blog.
items.promptEn: Samira lives with her daughter in a shared flat.
items.answerDe: Samira wohnt mit ihrer Tochter in einer Wohngemeinschaft.
items.rule: 'mit' + Dative: 'ihre Tochter' → 'mit ihrer Tochter' (feminine Dative -er). 'in einer Wohngemeinschaft' is location, Dative again. 'WG' is the universal abbreviation.
alternativeAnswers: Samira wohnt mit ihrer Tochter in einer WG.

items.context: Samira's daughter Leyla wants to know where to put the books.
items.promptEn: Put the books in the shelf. (informal, use 'stellen')
items.answerDe: Stell die Bücher ins Regal.
items.rule: Direction → Accusative: 'in das Regal' → 'ins Regal'. Books standing upright on a shelf are 'gestellt', not 'gelegt'. Plural 'die Bücher' is unchanged in the Accusative.
alternativeAnswers: Stell die Bücher in das Regal.
Stell die Bücher ins Regal!

lessons.storyArc: Second stop: Köln. On the street Nasrin finds an ID card and takes it to the police station at the main station, where she has to fill in a form. Just then an agitated woman rushes in – her ID is gone! The woman is so grateful she invites Nasrin for coffee. On the same day Nasrin has to phone the Ausländerbehörde in Hamburg to move the appointment for her residence-permit extension.
lessons.setting: Police station at Köln Hauptbahnhof; phone call to Hamburg
characters: the woman who lost her ID
grammarFocus: Subordinate clauses with wenn (verb at end)
Genitive with names (Minas Schule, Nasrins Ausweis)
Review: dies- in Nominativ and Akkusativ

items.context: Nasrin walks into the police station holding the ID card.
items.promptEn: I found this ID card on the street.
items.answerDe: Ich habe diesen Personalausweis auf der Straße gefunden.
items.rule: 'der Personalausweis' is masculine, and as the object of 'finden' it is Accusative: 'diesen'. 'auf der Straße' is a location → Dative. 'finden' is strong: 'gefunden'.
alternativeAnswers: Ich habe diesen Ausweis auf der Straße gefunden.

items.context: The officer explains the procedure and Nasrin repeats it to be sure.
items.promptEn: If someone finds an ID card, he has to take it to the police.
items.answerDe: Wenn man einen Ausweis findet, muss man ihn zur Polizei bringen.
items.rule: 'wenn' opens a subordinate clause, so its verb goes to the END ('findet'). When the wenn-clause comes first, it occupies position 1, so the main clause starts with the verb: ', muss man ...'. 'ihn' refers back to the masculine 'Ausweis'.
alternativeAnswers: Wenn man einen Personalausweis findet, muss man ihn zur Polizei bringen.

items.context: The officer hands her a form: 'Füllen Sie das bitte aus. Haben Sie noch Fragen?'
items.promptEn: Yes, do I have to fill in everything or only the first page?
items.answerDe: Ja, muss ich alles ausfüllen oder nur die erste Seite?
items.rule: 'alles' (everything) is a pronoun that never changes form. 'ausfüllen' is separable, but after the modal 'muss' the infinitive stays whole at the end. 'die erste Seite' – ordinal adjective after 'die' takes -e.

items.context: The woman bursts in shouting. The officer looks at the card in Nasrin's hand.
items.promptEn: That is this woman's ID card! (use 'Frau Meier')
items.answerDe: Das ist Frau Meiers Ausweis!
items.rule: With names, German shows possession by simply adding -s, with no apostrophe: 'Frau Meiers Ausweis', 'Minas Schule', 'Nasrins Welt'. The apostrophe is only used when the name already ends in s/z/x: 'Hans' Auto'.
alternativeAnswers: Das ist der Ausweis von Frau Meier!

items.context: Nasrin phones the Ausländerbehörde in Hamburg. The employee answers.
items.promptEn: Good morning, my name is Fani. I would like to postpone my appointment.
items.answerDe: Guten Morgen, mein Name ist Fani. Ich möchte meinen Termin verschieben.
items.rule: 'verschieben' (to postpone) has the inseparable prefix ver-. 'der Termin' is masculine → 'meinen Termin' in the Accusative. This sentence works for any office, doctor or hairdresser.
alternativeAnswers: Guten Morgen, Fani mein Name. Ich möchte meinen Termin verschieben.
Guten Morgen, mein Name ist Fani. Ich möchte gern meinen Termin verschieben.

items.context: The employee asks: 'Um welchen Termin geht es denn?'
items.promptEn: It's about the extension of my residence permit on the 12th of October.
items.answerDe: Es geht um die Verlängerung meiner Aufenthaltserlaubnis am zwölften Oktober.
items.rule: 'Es geht um' + Accusative = it's about. 'meiner Aufenthaltserlaubnis' is a Genitive (of my residence permit) – feminine Genitive ends in -er. Long compounds like 'Aufenthaltserlaubnis' are normal in official German; learn them as one chunk.
alternativeAnswers: Es geht um die Verlängerung meiner Aufenthaltserlaubnis am 12. Oktober.

items.context: Nasrin explains to the employee when she can come instead.
items.promptEn: If I'm back in Hamburg, I can come by any time.
items.answerDe: Wenn ich wieder in Hamburg bin, kann ich jederzeit vorbeikommen.
items.rule: Subordinate clause first: verb 'bin' at the end of the wenn-clause; then comma, then the main-clause verb 'kann' immediately. 'vorbeikommen' (to drop by) is separable but stays whole after a modal. 'jederzeit' = any time.
alternativeAnswers: Wenn ich wieder in Hamburg bin, kann ich jederzeit kommen.
